opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so that was something we went back and forth on a bit. The basic tension is that you want a high response rate, because if only, say, ten percent of people respond, you start worrying a lot about who those ten percent are. Maybe they're the people who are especially excited about AI, or especially worried about it, and then your results are skewed in ways you can't really correct for.

So paying people seemed like a pretty straightforward way to get more of them to take it seriously and actually fill it out. These are busy researchers, and we're asking for a decent chunk of their time on fairly hard questions. Fifty dollars isn't a lot for someone in machine learning, but it signals that we value their time, and it nudges people who would otherwise just ignore the email.

On the other side, there's a worry that payment changes who responds, or how carefully they respond. Maybe you pull in people who just want to click through quickly. And of course there's cost: when you're emailing thousands of people, it adds up.

In the end, I think we felt that the response-rate benefit was the bigger deal. Non-response bias is one of the main criticisms people raise about surveys like this, so anything that broadens who answers is pretty valuable. And in past rounds, we'd seen that offering payment did seem to help. So it seemed worth it, even if it's not a perfect fix for the selection issues.

r001.rationale: The response says payment seemed to help in past rounds, but does not describe a small initial comparison or say that its apparent effect motivated extending the $50 offer to everyone.

fable-5.1.text:
So, the first time we ran it, in 2016, we didn't pay anyone, and the response rate was something like twenty-one percent, which is pretty low. And the worry with a low response rate isn't just that you get fewer people, it's that the people who do respond might be different from the people who don't. If the only people who answer a survey about AI risk are the ones who already think about AI risk a lot, you've learned something, but not the thing you wanted to learn.

So when we did it again in 2022, we thought, what actually moves the needle on response rates? And the survey methodology literature is fairly clear that money helps, and that it helps more if it's unconditional, or at least not framed as a tiny wage for your time, but more as a kind of gesture of respect. Fifty dollars seemed like roughly the amount where a busy researcher goes, okay, that's at least a gift card, I'll do the twenty minutes, rather than a number that feels insulting or a number that's so large it's weird.

The other consideration was honestly just cost. We were contacting thousands of people who'd published at NeurIPS and ICML and so on. If a large fraction respond, fifty dollars each adds up fast. So it was a bit of a bet on how many would take it. And in practice the response rate did go up meaningfully, to around fifteen percent in 2023 out of a much larger pool, so I think it was worth it, though I'd love to be able to run the counterfactual where we didn't offer anything and see exactly how much was the money versus other changes we made.

There's also a slightly funny thing where a bunch of people declined the payment, or asked us to donate it, which I take as weak evidence that it was functioning more as a signal that we were serious than as the actual reason they participated.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the $50 offer was chosen based on survey-methodology literature, cost, and perceived respect. It does not describe a small initial comparison suggesting $50 improved participation or say that this result motivated extending the offer to everyone.

astra-6.text: The basic tradeoff was whether offering $50 would increase participation enough to justify the cost. These researchers’ time is valuable, so it’s not really payment at their usual hourly rate; it’s more a token of appreciation. And then there’s the question of who responds: ideally, an incentive gets you responses from people who wouldn’t otherwise participate, rather than just rewarding the people who were going to answer anyway. So the relevant comparison is how many additional responses you get, and whether they make the survey more representative.

r001.rationale: The response describes weighing the cost against added participation, but does not mention a small initial comparison suggesting $50 improved participation or that this prompted offering it to everyone.

AI researchers are busy, so $50 probably isn’t going to compensate them fully for their time, but it might make the request feel more worth responding to. And getting more responses matters because you worry that the people who choose to answer are systematically different from those who don’t. Of course, payment could also change who responds, so a higher response rate doesn’t automatically mean a more representative sample.
